cc: Gradual tingling and numbness in both feet

HPI: 28-year-old man with gradually progressive tingling, burning and reduced sensation beginning in both toes; onset 4 months ago. Spread to ankles, not hands; now daily. Burning is 5/10 at night and aggravated by bedsheet contact; removing the sheet helps. Foot cream ineffective. Increased thirst. No injury or previous similar symptoms.

Perspective: Will I lose my feet like someone I know?

PMH: Type 2 diabetes — they diagnosed me at 18, about ten years ago; and my last A1c was high, though I don't remember the number.

PSH: No surgery or admissions.

Meds: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; sometimes misses evening dose when work runs late.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked. One alcoholic drink monthly; no recreational drugs. Cashier standing most of an 8-hour shift in close-fitting work shoes. Lives with wife; unrestricted diet.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has diabetes.; My father's fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have a brother who's thirty-one, and he's healthy.; As far as I know, nerve problems like this don't run in my family.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports numbness. Reports paresthesia. Denies weakness. General - Reports polydipsia. Denies weight loss. Denies fever. Gastrointestinal - Denies diarrhea. Denies constipation. Denies nausea.
note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable at rest.
Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: In the examined posterior fields, clear breath sounds bilaterally.
Neurologic: Reduced light touch and vibration symmetrically from toes to ankles.
Neurologic: Achilles reflexes reduced bilaterally; patellar reflexes 2+.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.
Skin: Skin of feet intact, without visible ulceration.
Heart: Dorsalis pedis pulses palpable and symmetric.
Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
P: 1. Assess symmetric sensory loss, foot integrity and gait; obtain A1c and review diabetes management and renal function; discuss individualized neuropathic-pain treatment with clinician review, daily foot checks and protective footwear; follow up in 2–4 weeks and seek prompt care for wounds, rapidly progressive weakness or falls. Review shoe fit and plan the evening dose around work with the patient.
2. Check B12 and CBC, particularly with long-term metformin use; replace a confirmed deficiency and investigate its cause; explain that more than one contributor may coexist.

3. Review neurotoxic drugs, supplements and alcohol exposure; do not stop necessary medication without prescriber review; arrange further neurologic testing if the pattern is atypical or progresses. Refer to neurology for atypical or progressive deficits and consider nerve conduction studies when needed to clarify the pattern; educate the patient to review supplements and drug exposures with the prescribing clinician rather than stopping necessary treatment independently.

cc: Gradual tingling and numbness in both feet

HPI: 28-year-old man with gradually progressive tingling, burning and reduced sensation beginning in both toes; onset 4 months ago. Spread to ankles, not hands; now daily. Burning is 5/10 at night and aggravated by bedsheet contact; removing the sheet helps. Foot cream ineffective. Increased thirst. No injury or previous similar symptoms.

Perspective: Will I lose my feet like someone I know?

PMH: Type 2 diabetes — they diagnosed me at 18, about ten years ago; and my last A1c was high, though I don't remember the number.

PSH: No surgery or admissions.

Meds: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; sometimes misses evening dose when work runs late.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked. One alcoholic drink monthly; no recreational drugs. Cashier standing most of an 8-hour shift in close-fitting work shoes. Lives with wife; unrestricted diet.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has diabetes.; My father's fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have a brother who's thirty-one, and he's healthy.; As far as I know, nerve problems like this don't run in my family.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports numbness. Reports paresthesia. Denies weakness. General - Reports polydipsia. Denies weight loss. Denies fever. Gastrointestinal - Denies diarrhea. Denies constipation. Denies nausea.

Patient concern: I cannot see the bottoms of my feet clearly.

P: 1. Assess symmetric sensory loss, foot integrity and gait; obtain A1c and review diabetes management and renal function; discuss individualized neuropathic-pain treatment with clinician review, daily foot checks and protective footwear; follow up in 2–4 weeks and seek prompt care for wounds, rapidly progressive weakness or falls. Demonstrate using a mirror or a trusted helper with consent and have the patient choose a daily inspection routine. Review shoe fit and plan the evening dose around work with the patient.
2. Check B12 and CBC, particularly with long-term metformin use; replace a confirmed deficiency and investigate its cause; explain that more than one contributor may coexist.

3. Review neurotoxic drugs, supplements and alcohol exposure; do not stop necessary medication without prescriber review; arrange further neurologic testing if the pattern is atypical or progresses. Refer to neurology for atypical or progressive deficits and consider nerve conduction studies when needed to clarify the pattern; educate the patient to review supplements and drug exposures with the prescribing clinician rather than stopping necessary treatment independently.
